analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent federal protections for renters facing eviction after their home is foreclosed.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 45 House Democrats, was referred to the Financial Services Committee and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: When a rented home is foreclosed, a 2009 federal law requires the new owner to honor existing leases, or give tenants at least 90 days' notice before making them leave. That law had an expiration date. This bill would have removed the expiration date so the protections never run out, and would have let tenants sue in court — with attorneys' fees paid by the violator — when the rules are ignored. The bill never received any action after being referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters living in homes that go into foreclosure. Under the 2009 law the bill would have made permanent, a tenant with a lease could stay until the lease ends, and a month-to-month tenant had to get at least 90 days' notice before eviction. Section 8 voucher tenants would keep the same protections under the housing voucher program. The new private right of action means a tenant who is wrongfully evicted could recover damages in court, not just file a complaint.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the sunset date in the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act of 2009, so tenant protections would no longer expire.
Adds a private right of action: a tenant harmed by a violation can sue for damages and other relief, and a winning plaintiff is awarded attorneys' fees and litigation costs.

Under the underlying 2009 law being extended, a purchaser of a foreclosed rental home must honor existing leases and give tenants at least 90 days' notice to vacate — this bill makes those rules permanent and enforceable in court.

analysis.who_pays: Purchasers of foreclosed homes — investors, banks, and others who take title at foreclosure. They would have to honor remaining lease terms or provide 90 days' notice, which limits how quickly they can take over, resell, or re-rent the property, and a new right to sue with fee-shifting could raise their legal costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a private right of action with mandatory award of attorneys' fees and expert witness fees to prevailing tenants, which would expose purchasers of foreclosed property — including small landlords who buy foreclosed homes — to litigation costs and damage claims.

Buyers of foreclosed property would face uncertainty about occupancy: a lease that runs months or years longer can reduce what they are willing to bid at a foreclosure sale, which can mean lower proceeds for the defaulted borrower and the lender. This is the trade-off an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to tenants is substantial and targeted at a moment of genuine crisis — losing a home they paid for because someone else defaulted. The cost falls on a narrow group, purchasers of foreclosed property, and is real but manageable: honoring a lease or giving 90 days' notice is a limited delay, and fee-shifting applies only to violations. The design is straightforward, though the fee-shifting provision could invite disputes with buyers who claim they were unaware of a tenancy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never scheduled it for a hearing or a vote, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Keith Ellison introduced the bill on November 20, 2013, joined by 44 cosponsors, all Democrats.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day it was introduced.
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no mark-up, no floor vote — before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Purchasers of foreclosed homes — including investors who buy them to resell or rent — kept the flexibility to evict tenants quickly, since the protections were never made permanent. Tenants in foreclosed homes were left without a federal right to stay through their lease or a way to sue.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill to extend tenant foreclosure protections permanently.

sides.party_line_note: All 45 initial supporters — the sponsor and 44 cosponsors — were Democrats, no Republican signed on, and no vote was ever taken to test broader support.

industries.industry: Investors and buyers of foreclosed homes
industries.note: The bill would require anyone taking title to a foreclosed rental to honor existing leases or give tenants 90 days' notice, and would expose them to lawsuits with fee-shifting for violations. Their gain from quick eviction is the tenant's loss of housing, so their interest runs against the public here.
